source_uncertainties: Slide error (L19 f0022, joint PDFs): the mean of Q(U1,U2) is written with Q(U1,U2) inside the integral instead of Q(V1,V2) and ends with '= 1'; the spoken explanation (809-816 s) says 'this is not equal to 1'. The chapter gives the corrected form (7.16) and names both errors.

Slide error (L19 f0030, correlation coefficient) and spoken (1059-1078 s): rho12 = -1 called 'perfectly uncorrelated'. The T1 practice-problem slide (fgMG7Jd89pw f0065) has 'perfectly negatively correlated'. The chapter uses the latter and names the error.

Slide wording (L18 f0016): 'CDF is always increasing' corrected to non-decreasing (the joint-CDF slide L19 f0006 says non-decreasing); 'f(-inf) = f(inf) = 0' stated as true for the examples but not implied by normalization.

Slide figure labels (L19 f0038, Figure 3.17): the two curves are labelled 'Joint PDF f12(V1,V2)'. Both peak at about 0.2, at V2 about -1 and -9. For a jointly normal pair with the caption moments (means 1 and -1, variances 2 and 12, rho12 = -sqrt(2/3)) the conditional PDFs f2|1 have peaks 0.199 at -1 and -9, while slices of f12 would peak at 0.056 and 0.0010. The chapter states that the curves are conditional PDFs, as the spoken explanation says (1270-1292 s).

Slide figure (L19 f0038, Figure 3.16): the scatter has almost no points with V1 < 0, whereas a Gaussian U1 with mean 1 and variance 2 would put about 24 % there. The scatter may not be from the distribution in its caption; the chapter uses only the caption moments.

Slide figure (L19 f0009, Figure 3.13): caption <u2^2> = 5/16 (read from an enlarged crop; transcript 566 s also says 5 over 16), but the plotted V2 values span about -2 to 4, which suggests a larger variance. Not used for any derived number.
Slide gap (L18 f0046): the two-valued CDF is given for V <= a, a < V < b and V > b; V = b is unassigned. The chapter assigns F(b) = p from the strict inequality in F(V) = P{U < V} and says so.

Spoken slips, corrected in reader text with attribution: 'sigma of slightly close to 3' for the standardized Gaussian (L18 1207-1217 s; the axis spans -3 to 3); exponential support 'V greater than or equal to lambda' (L18 1099-1106 s; slide and figure start at V = 0); below rho* the variables 'tend to 0' (L17 1329-1345 s; Lorenz p. 135: true only for r < 1; for 1 < r < 24.74 the stable states are the nonzero steady-convection points); for independent variables 'you cannot have a joint PDF' (L19 1496-1500 s).

Slide value rho* approximately 25 (L17 f0046) is Lorenz's 470/19 = 24.74 (p. 136), the linear-stability threshold of the steady-convection states; the chapter does not extend it to a statement about all trajectories.
Slide term 'characterization function' (L18 f0031) is the characteristic function; slide term 'kurtosis' is written 'flatness' with the slide term given once.
The slide for practice problem L58-P4 calls U a 'stationary random variable'; the chapter notes that stationarity is not needed for the identity.
Practice-problem transcript doubt (T1, 31:15-31:26): the sixth Gaussian moment is heard as '50'; slide and recurrence give 15. Not mentioned in reader text.

Lecture-stated items attributed, not checked against a source: lecture's explanation that viscous diffusion damps perturbations in laminar flow (qualified in text by chapter 4's instability); use of log-normal and gamma PDFs for mixture fraction and species in combustion; the conditional temperature PDF on the stoichiometric mixture fraction in jet flames; computer precision as a perturbation source.

Lorenz-ensemble statistics change between t* = 60 and t* = 100 (variance 57.8 against 61.6, about 2.5 standard errors of the difference). A helper run to t* = 200 (not in the listing; _editorial/tmp/ch07_explore2.py) gave variances 62.9 at 150 and 63.7 at 200. The chapter makes no claim about long-time limits and points to chapter 8 (stationarity).
The two-run separation time depends on the time step (31.0 at dt = 0.01, 29.0 at dt = 0.005); the chapter reports both and calls the agreement with the slide's 't = 35' a consistency check.

ASR spellings corrected (slide text and standard spelling): 'Lawrence', 'Lorentz' = Lorenz; 'row 1 2' = rho12; 'belt curve' = bell curve; 'heavy side' = Heaviside; 'Cauchy-Schwartz' (slide spelling) = Cauchy-Schwarz; 'u bar the angle bracket' = <U>; 'VP' = V_b; 'joined normal' = jointly normal; 'F21' = f2|1.
Timestamps are section anchors from local speech-recognition segment times; they locate topic changes to within a few seconds.

sections.section: The objects of the chapter and the running case
sections.lecture_material: Repeated experiment under conditions C; sample-space variable V (slide notation).
sections.teaching_construction: Formal model of the repeatable experiment; relative-frequency interpretation of probability; ensemble average; the chapter 6 air-jet station (mean 8 m/s, r.m.s. 2 m/s) as running case with a Gaussian model; the Lorenz ensemble as computable example.

sections.section: Repeated experiments make the velocity a random variable
sections.lecture_material: Module introduction (means, variances, higher moments); source slide (Pope 2000); Figure 3.1 sketch of U^(n) over about 40 repetitions; event A = {U < 10 m/s} neither certain nor impossible; U a random variable.
sections.teaching_construction: P{U < 10 m/s} = 0.841 under the Gaussian model; binomial standard deviation 0.037 for 100 runs as a test of a probability prediction.

sections.section: Repeated experiments make the velocity a random variable (continued)
sections.lecture_material: For laminar flow U is calculated accurately; for turbulent flow U is unpredictable; the theory predicts probabilities; 'seemingly random'.

sections.section: Deterministic equations, incomplete conditions and sensitivity
sections.lecture_material: Consistency of random outcomes with deterministic Navier-Stokes equations; two reasons: perturbations in ICs, BCs and material properties, and sensitivity; examples (pipe roughness, impurities); viscous damping in laminar flow; computer precision in simulations.
sections.teaching_construction: Qualification by chapter 4: only a stable laminar flow returns to its state; rounding as a perturbation; 'random' as a property of outcomes under incomplete conditions.

sections.section: Lorenz's equations: sensitivity to the initial state in three variables
sections.lecture_material: Lorenz equations with sigma = 10, beta = 8/3, rho = 28; initial conditions 0.1 and 0.100001; Figure 3.2 (indistinguishable at first, quite different by t = 35); unpredictability; dependence on coefficients, rho* about 25.
sections.research_extension: Lorenz 1963: abstract (p. 130); equations (25)-(27), meaning of X, Y, Z, Pr, r, b, and the truncation limit (p. 135); origin stable for r < 1, steady states +/- sqrt(b(r-1)), r - 1 (p. 135); critical r = 470/19 = 24.74, parameter values, steady states (+/-6 sqrt 2, +/-6 sqrt 2, 27) (p. 136).
sections.teaching_construction: Notation Pr, r, beta; correction of 'tend to 0'; computed separation time 31.0 / 29.0 by time step; the Lorenz ensemble (N = 4000, window 1e-5, dt = 0.01, t* = 100) as a random variable produced without a random-number generator.

sections.section: The cumulative distribution function and the probability density function
sections.lecture_material: Recap; sample space and the events B and C (Figure 3.4); CDF F(V) = P{U < V}; P(C) = F(Vb) - F(Va); three properties; PDF as derivative; non-negative, normalized; probability as integral; PDF fully characterizes U; identically distributed variables; jet sample-space example.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of (7.4) from disjoint events; non-decreasing versus increasing; f(+/-inf) = 0 not implied; units of f and f > 1 (jet: 0.199 s/m = 0.055 h/km; Lorenz t* = 20); empirical CDF and histogram estimate; Figure 7.1 (computed).

sections.lecture_material: Mean, fluctuation, variance, central moments mu_n, mu_0 = 1, mu_1 = 0, mu_2 = sigma^2; standardized variable and PDF; standardized moments, skewness, kurtosis; characteristic function and Fourier pair.
sections.research_extension: Wilczek, Daitche, Friedrich 2011 (arXiv pp. 2, 14, 25): velocity PDF similar to Gaussian with sub-Gaussian tails; central-limit argument 'rather hand-waving'. Kerr 1983 (NASA TM 84407 pp. 1, 2, 15, 17, 35): derivative skewness -0.505 +/- 0.005, not increasing with Re; derivative flatness 3.39 to 5.11 for R_lambda 9.0 to 82.9; low Re of simulations. Yeung, Sreenivasan, Pope 2018 (p. 064603-6): longitudinal gradients negatively skewed, transverse symmetric and more non-Gaussian; dissipation fluctuations to several thousand times the mean.
sections.teaching_construction: Change-of-variables derivation of the standardized PDF; tail condition m > n + 1 for existence of moments; Cauchy example; properties of Psi; Lorenz ensemble moments at t* = 60 and 100 with standard errors; rule of use for Gaussian reference values.

sections.section: Standard PDFs: uniform, exponential, Gaussian, log-normal, gamma and discrete
sections.lecture_material: Uniform, exponential (Figure 3.6), Gaussian and standardized Gaussian (Figure 3.7, F(-1) = 0.159, F(-2) = 0.023), log-normal (Figure 3.8, <Y> = 1, var 1/20, 1/2, 5), gamma (Figure 3.9, alpha = (mu/sigma)^2, f(0) zero or infinite), two-valued discrete with Heaviside CDF and delta PDF, sure variable; velocities not usually gamma or log-normal; use in species transport and combustion.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 7.1 (moments; checked numerically by _editorial/tmp/ch07_numbers.py); sigma^2 = ln(1 + var Y) values; alpha = 20, 2, 0.2; H(0) = 0 convention; delta-function rule; flatness lower bound 1; running-case probabilities 0.841, 0.683, 3.2e-5 with the tail caveat.

sections.section: Two random variables: joint CDF, joint PDF and marginals
sections.lecture_material: Velocity vector and sample-space vector; joint CDF; non-decreasing; F12(-inf, V2) = 0; marginal CDF; scatter plot of a jointly normal pair (Figure 3.13); joint PDF; rectangle probability; marginal PDF; mean of Q(U1,U2); means and variances from marginals.
sections.teaching_construction: Units of the joint PDF; correction of the slide's mean formula; empirical joint CDF from a scatter; marginals do not determine the joint PDF.

sections.lecture_material: Covariance as mixed second moment; correlation coefficient; signs; -1 <= rho12 <= 1 by Cauchy-Schwarz; uncorrelated and perfectly correlated.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of |rho12| <= 1 and its equality case; correction of 'perfectly uncorrelated'; symmetry arguments for zero covariance (jet axis, Lorenz (x,y,z) -> (-x,-y,z)); Lorenz rho_xz = 0.023 with dependence shown by conditional means 18.2 and 31.9.

sections.lecture_material: Conditional PDF f2|1 = f12/f1; normalization; undefined where f1 = 0; conditional mean; Figures 3.16 and 3.17; combustion application; independence and factorization.
sections.teaching_construction: Normalization proof; independence implies zero correlation; bivariate normal PDF, factorization at rho12 = 0; marginal of the bivariate normal derived by integrating over V2 (Gaussian with sigma_1 for every rho12); conditional PDF (7.23) and its mean and variance (7.24) by completing the square; Figure 3.17 identified as conditional PDFs (computation in Exercise 3).

sections.section: Executable ensemble: a deterministic system sampled as a random variable
sections.lecture_material: Lorenz equations and initial conditions from L17.
sections.teaching_construction: NumPy RK4 ensemble: two-run separation at two time steps; ensemble at t* = 20, 60, 100; moments, standard errors, empirical CDF, histogram, correlations, conditional means; two assertions (histogram normalization, |rho| <= 1); neighbour-correlation and step-halving checks; zero-window failure test.

sections.section: What the probabilistic description establishes and what it does not
sections.research_extension: Wilczek et al. 2011; Kerr 1983; Yeung, Sreenivasan, Pope 2018; Lorenz 1963 p. 135.
sections.teaching_construction: Classification of definitions, derivations and conditional results; ensemble versus time average with stationarity and ergodicity named (chapter 8); scope of the Gaussian model and of the Lorenz ensemble.

sections.lecture_material: Exercises 7-11 are adapted from the course practice problems L57-P3 (7UyTD2lT0sI 16:18), L58-P4 (nBZWHP4w8fY 0:21), L60-P12 (8-WExK8ejdQ 17:39), T1-P3 (fgMG7Jd89pw 24:35) and T1-P4 (fgMG7Jd89pw 31:52), as assigned by _editorial/practice-map.md.
sections.research_extension: Exercise 5 uses Kerr's flatness; Exercise 4 uses the dissipation-PDF statement of Yeung et al.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises (check an assumption, counterexample, compute, counterexample, design, judge a claim) and full solutions for all eleven.

references.title: Lorenz 1963, Deterministic nonperiodic flow (J. Atmos. Sci. 20, 130-141)
references.supports: p. 130 abstract: 'nonperiodic solutions are ordinarily unstable with respect to small modifications, so that slightly differing initial states can evolve into considerably different states'. p. 135: equations (25)-(27); X proportional to the intensity of convective motion, Y to the temperature difference between ascending and descending currents, Z to the distortion of the vertical temperature profile; sigma the Prandtl number, r = Ra/Rc; 'their solutions cannot be expected to resemble those of (17) and (18) when strong convection occurs, in view of the extreme truncation'; origin: all roots negative when r < 1; steady states X = Y = +/- sqrt(b(r-1)), Z = r - 1. p. 136: eq. (34) critical r; sigma = 10, b = 8/3, critical r = 470/19 = 24.74; r = 28; steady states (+/-6 sqrt 2, +/-6 sqrt 2, 27). Scanned PDF from the MIT Lorenz archive (wind.mit.edu/~emanuel/Lorenz/EdLorenz/Deterministic_63.pdf); pages rendered and read.

references.title: Wilczek, Daitche, Friedrich 2011, On the velocity distribution in homogeneous isotropic turbulence (J. Fluid Mech. 676, 191-217; arXiv:1107.0139v1)
references.supports: p. 2: the central-limit argument for a Gaussian velocity PDF 'turns out to be rather hand-waving as the assumption of statistical independence is obviously violated'; vorticity PDF has extremely non-Gaussian tails. p. 14: 'although the PDF is similar to Gaussian, significant deviations occur. Especially notable is the sub-Gaussian tail, which has also been found in experiments and other numerical simulations'. p. 25: 'the velocity PDF displays slight deviations from a Gaussian distribution with sub-Gaussian tails'.
references.page_checked: arXiv preprint pp. 2, 14, 25 (PDF pp. 2, 14, 25); journal pagination not checked

references.title: Kerr 1983, Higher-order derivative correlations and the alignment of small-scale structures in isotropic numerical turbulence (NASA TM 84407)
references.supports: p. 1 (abstract): velocity- and mixed-derivative skewnesses do not increase with Reynolds number; R_lambda to 82.9. p. 2: limited range of scales 'restricts the Reynolds number to very low values'. p. 15: 'The value for the velocity-derivative skewness for simulations F11 to F27 is -0.505 +/- 0.005.' p. 17: F1 equals the velocity-derivative flatness if isotropy is assumed. p. 35, Table 3: F1 = 3.39 at R_lambda = 9.0 and 5.11 at 82.9; S_u from -0.497 to -0.523 over the forced runs F1-F27.
references.page_checked: TM p. 1 (PDF p. 3); p. 2 (PDF p. 4); p. 15 (PDF p. 17); p. 17 (PDF p. 19); p. 35 (PDF p. 37)

references.title: Yeung, Sreenivasan, Pope 2018, Effects of finite spatial and temporal resolution in DNS (Phys. Rev. Fluids 3, 064603)
references.supports: p. 064603-6: 'longitudinal velocity gradients are negatively skewed but transverse gradients, while symmetric, are more strongly non-Gaussian'; improved resolution reduces 'the likelihood of large fluctuations up to several thousands times the mean value' of dissipation and enstrophy.
references.page_checked: p. 064603-6 (PDF p. 6), author copy at tcg.mae.cornell.edu
